reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Typically an insidious, painless, bilateral (often asymmetric) chronic optic neuropathy detected on screening rather than by symptoms
Peripheral visual field is lost first, with central acuity preserved until late, so patients are frequently unaware until damage is advanced
The drainage angle is open on gonioscopy, distinguishing it from angle-closure disease
Hallmark disc changes include increased cup-to-disc ratio, focal neuroretinal rim thinning or notching, and disc haemorrhages
Risk rises with elevated intraocular pressure, older age, family history, African ancestry, high myopia, and thin central corneas
Normal-tension glaucoma shows characteristic optic nerve and field damage despite pressures in the statistically normal range
Management aims to lower intraocular pressure with topical medication first, escalating to laser trabeculoplasty or surgical drainage (trabeculectomy) to slow progression
reference.pathophysiology: Primary open-angle glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy in which aqueous outflow through an anatomically open trabecular meshwork is impaired, raising resistance to drainage. The resulting intraocular pressure, sometimes within the normal range, contributes to mechanical and vascular stress at the optic nerve head, causing loss of retinal ganglion cell axons. This produces characteristic cupping of the optic disc and a corresponding pattern of arcuate and peripheral visual field loss that advances slowly over years.
additionalInvestigations: Applanation tonometry to measure intraocular pressure
Gonioscopy to confirm the angle is open
Dilated optic disc examination for cupping and rim changes
Automated perimetry (visual field testing) to detect and monitor field loss
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex
Central corneal thickness (pachymetry), which influences pressure interpretation and risk
redFlags: Progressive visual field loss or disc change despite apparently controlled pressure
Disc (splinter) haemorrhage, a marker of ongoing progression
Very high presenting pressure or advanced cupping threatening fixation
Rapid deterioration suggesting a secondary or aggressive glaucoma
reference.prognosis: With early detection and sustained pressure control most patients retain useful vision for life, but untreated or poorly controlled disease progresses to irreversible visual field loss and blindness.
pitfalls: Relying on a single pressure reading, as pressure fluctuates and can be normal in normal-tension glaucoma
Attributing all disc cupping to glaucoma without correlating fields and nerve fibre layer
Poor adherence to topical therapy going unrecognised as the cause of progression
Overlooking secondary causes such as pseudoexfoliation or long-term steroid use
management: Topical prostaglandin analogue such as latanoprost as first-line therapy to lower intraocular pressure, the only modifiable risk factor
Additional pressure-lowering drops including beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or rho-kinase inhibitors, added or substituted to reach the target pressure
Selective laser trabeculoplasty as a first-line alternative or adjunct to medical therapy
Incisional or minimally invasive glaucoma surgery, such as trabeculectomy or a drainage device, for progression despite maximal tolerated medical treatment
Regular monitoring with applanation tonometry, optic disc and retinal nerve fibre layer imaging, and automated perimetry to detect progression
Support for adherence and correct drop technique, with patient education on the asymptomatic nature of early disease
Ongoing ophthalmology follow-up with low-vision support and rehabilitation for advanced visual loss

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Primary open-angle glaucoma

nodes.text: Suspected primary open-angle glaucoma: raised IOP, cupping or field loss
Progression despite controlled IOP, disc haemorrhage or advanced cupping?
Escalate: urgent ophthalmology review for rapid or secondary glaucoma
Applanation tonometry; gonioscopy; disc examination; perimetry; RNFL OCT; pachymetry
Do disc, field and OCT findings confirm glaucomatous damage with an open angle?
Consider ocular hypertension or non-glaucomatous neuropathy; reassess
Latanoprost as first-line therapy to lower intraocular pressure
Add beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, CAIs or rho-kinase inhibitors
Selective laser trabeculoplasty as first-line alternative or adjunct
Trabeculectomy or drainage device if progression despite medical therapy
Lifelong monitoring of pressure, disc, RNFL and fields; low-vision support if advanced
